You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 Drafting Review: Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Enforcement Gaps

Issues are listed in section order. Items 34–39 cover things missing from the bill entirely.

### Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton cap applies "by a single vessel," so an operator could spread recovery across several vessels, each under the cap, with no limit on the total. There is no aggregation rule by operator, project, or affiliate.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "per year."** The bill doesn't say whether this means a calendar year, a fiscal year, or any rolling 12-month period. An operator could time recovery around the boundary.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), how tonnage is measured.** The bill doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry, or whether it counts sediment and water lifted with the ore. Freshly recovered nodules carry substantial water, so the choice could change compliance significantly.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery."** The term is undefined. It's unclear whether collecting and disturbing the seabed without lifting material to the surface, or lifting and discarding material, counts.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "from the seabed."** The bill doesn't say whether it covers material cut from the subsoil, which matters for seafloor massive sulfides and cobalt crusts. "Other mineral resources" is also undefined and could arguably reach sand and gravel dredging or other deep extraction the sponsors may not intend.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A), geographic scope.** The bill never says where the prohibition applies: state waters, the U.S. EEZ and continental shelf, areas beyond national jurisdiction, or other nations' waters. Depth is the only spatial limit.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "vessel."** Modern systems use a surface ship plus a seafloor collector and riser. It's unclear which is the "vessel," and operations using a fixed or semi-submersible platform might not count as a vessel at all.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** The bill never defines which Secretary (Commerce? Interior?). That creates uncertainty about who can expand the definition and invites challenge to any determination.

9. **Sec. 2(1)(B), open-ended delegation.** "Poses risks … comparable to" has no standards, procedures, or rulemaking requirement. Courts no longer defer to agency readings of ambiguous statutes (*Loper Bright*, 2024), which makes these determinations easier to attack.

10. **Sec. 2(1)(B) with Sec. 5(b), criminal liability.** Because willful violations carry up to 10 years, letting a Secretary define criminal conduct by an open-ended "comparable risk" test invites void-for-vagueness and nondelegation challenges.

11. **Sec. 2(2), entity types.** The definition covers only citizens and "corporations." It omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other non-corporate entities, so a company could restructure as an LLC to fall outside extraterritorial coverage.

12. **Sec. 2(2), "State."** "State" is undefined and may not include the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, or the territories, so entities organized there might not be covered.

13. **Sec. 2(2), foreign subsidiaries and residents.** Foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies are not covered, nor are lawful permanent residents or U.S. nationals who aren't citizens. A U.S. parent could run mining through a foreign-incorporated affiliate.

14. **Sec. 2(3), size threshold.** Mining-capable vessels under 5,000 gross tons escape registration entirely. "Equipped for the recovery" is also ambiguous, since equipment can be installed or removed between voyages.

15. **Sec. 2(3) vs. Sec. 2(1)(A), mismatched triggers.** The registry turns on vessel size, while the prohibition turns on annual tonnage recovered. Small vessels could mine without registering, and large vessels doing exempt work have no tonnage-reporting requirement tied to the prohibition.

### Sec. 3: Prohibition

16. **Sec. 3(a), "engage in."** It's unclear whether financing, chartering, owning, sponsoring, or contracting for mining counts. There is no aiding-and-abetting or conspiracy language specific to the Act.

17. **Sec. 3(a), no trade or processing provisions.** Nothing bars importing, processing, or selling seabed-mined minerals in the U.S. Foreign-flagged or foreign-sponsored operators, including those working under other nations' sponsorship, could mine and sell into the U.S. market.

18. **Sec. 3(b), scope of the grandfather clause.** The exemption covers "mining conducted under an exploration license." Exploration licenses don't normally authorize commercial recovery, so the bill is ambiguous: it either exempts very little or arguably authorizes commercial-scale mining under an exploration license.

19. **Sec. 3(b), which licenses.** The bill doesn't say whether "license" means only NOAA licenses under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA), or also International Seabed Authority contracts or foreign-state licenses.

20. **Sec. 3(b), no limits on the grandfather.** There is no expiration date, tonnage cap, or rule on renewals, extensions, transfers, or amendments. A license could be sold or expanded and still claim the exemption indefinitely.

21. **Sec. 3(c), "environmental assessment."** The term is undefined, with no tonnage cap, permit, approval, or certification process. Because the test is "purpose," an operator could label large-scale test mining as assessment.

### Sec. 4: Registry

22. **Sec. 4, no penalty.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3. Failing to register, failing to report, or filing a false report carries no penalty under the Act; only general statutes such as 18 U.S.C. § 1001 might apply.

23. **Sec. 4(a), no deadline and undefined "operator."** There is no registration deadline. "Operator" is undefined (owner, charterer, or master?), so responsibility can be disputed.

24. **Sec. 4(a), foreign vessels.** It's unclear whether foreign-flagged covered vessels must register, or what jurisdictional hook would apply to them.

25. **Sec. 4(b), no required content.** Reports need not include tonnage, location, depth, or the exemption claimed. That makes them of limited use for proving a Sec. 3 violation or verifying a 3(b) or 3(c) claim.

26. **Sec. 4, no verification authority.** Reports are self-certified. NOAA gets no inspection, monitoring, observer, vessel-tracking, subpoena, or rulemaking authority to check them.

### Sec. 5: Penalties

27. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8, timing conflict.** Sec. 5(a) applies penalties to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 8 makes the Act effective 180 days later. That creates a direct conflict over the 180-day window and possible fair-notice or retroactivity challenges.

28. **Sec. 5(a), daily penalty vs. annual threshold.** A violation depends on exceeding an annual tonnage, so it's unclear on which "day" the violation occurs. It could be the day the threshold is crossed, every day of that year, or only days after crossing it.

29. **Sec. 5(a), no enforcement machinery.** No agency is designated to assess penalties. There are no procedures for notice, hearing, or judicial review. After *SEC v. Jarkesy* (2024), administratively imposed civil penalties may face Seventh Amendment jury-trial challenges.

30. **Sec. 5, missing remedies.** There is no injunctive relief, seizure or forfeiture of vessels or cargo, permit sanctions, or citizen-suit provision. Enforcement depends entirely on after-the-fact monetary or criminal penalties.

### Sec. 6: International Agreement

31. **Sec. 6, ambiguous deadline.** It's unclear whether the 18-month deadline applies to starting or concluding negotiations. "Seek to negotiate" is not judicially enforceable, and there is no reporting requirement. The provision also doesn't address U.S. non-ratification of UNCLOS or the ISA process.

### Sec. 7: Duration

32. **Sec. 7(a) vs. Sec. 7(b), internal conflict.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress acts, while (b) ends the whole Act after 10 years regardless. The (a) mechanism is also redundant, since a joint resolution requires presentment and is effectively new legislation. Nothing directs or funds NASEM to produce the triggering report.

33. **Sec. 7(b), no savings clause.** The bill doesn't say whether pending enforcement actions for pre-sunset violations survive expiration. Applying the general savings statute (1 U.S.C. § 109) to an expiring rather than repealed act is not clearly settled.

### Missing from the bill

34. **Conflict with existing licensing law.** The bill doesn't amend or reconcile DSHMRA, under which NOAA licenses and permits deep seabed hard mineral recovery. Nor does it address hard-mineral leasing under OCSLA § 8(k). Agencies could arguably keep issuing licenses and permits, and conflicting statutes invite litigation.

35. **No severability clause.** Given the legally vulnerable Sec. 2(1)(B) delegation, a successful challenge could put other provisions at risk.

36. **No general rulemaking authority.** No agency is directed to issue implementing regulations for definitions, measurement, exemptions, or reporting.

37. **No authorization of appropriations.** No funding is provided for NOAA's registry, enforcement, or the NASEM study.

38. **No anti-evasion clause.** Nothing addresses structuring, splitting, or reorganizing activities to avoid thresholds (see items 1, 11, and 13).

39. **No relationship to state waters.** The bill doesn't address preemption or overlap with state-waters jurisdiction.

---

**Notes for coverage:**
- Check this against the official manager's amendment text on Congress.gov before publishing. Sec. 5(a)'s enactment-date language and the Sec. 3(b) wording are the items most likely to have changed.
- To keep with CPR's nonpartisan approach, it may help to frame these as "questions the text leaves open" and get responses from committee staff on both sides. Some gaps, such as the per-vessel threshold or the narrow U.S. person definition, may be deliberate compromises rather than drafting errors.
- The *Loper Bright*, *Jarkesy*, and savings-statute points are worth confirming with an administrative or ocean law expert before quoting them as likely outcomes.
